title: Genome organisation and size
summary: How much DNA, and what is in it.

layers.basics: Genomes range from ≈ 160 kb in small bacterial symbionts to > 100 Gb in some plants. Bacteria have compact, gene-dense genomes; eukaryotes carry large amounts of noncoding DNA.
layers.deeper: The "C-value paradox" notes that genome size does not track organismal complexity: onions have ≈ 5× more DNA than humans.
layers.expert: Genome size correlates with cell size and division time and is shaped by transposon expansion and drift (Lynch). Human genome: ≈ 1.5% coding, ≈ 45% transposon-derived, ≈ 8% from retroviral insertions.

layers.basics: Mitochondria carry their own circular DNA, inherited almost entirely from the mother. Human mtDNA codes for 13 proteins, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs.
layers.deeper: Cells hold many copies; a mix of normal and mutant copies is called heteroplasmy. Mitochondrial diseases appear when mutant copies exceed a threshold (often ≈ 60–90%).
layers.expert: mtDNA has a higher mutation rate (≈ 10–20× nuclear) and slightly different genetic code. mtDNA is used for maternal-lineage studies and ancient DNA (e.g., Neanderthal mtDNA).

layers.basics: Riboswitches are RNA segments in mRNAs that change shape when they bind a small molecule, turning a gene on or off. Ribozymes are RNAs that act as enzymes.
layers.deeper: Examples: the thiamine pyrophosphate riboswitch in bacteria; self-splicing introns and RNase P. Cech and Altman won the 1989 Nobel.
layers.expert: Riboswitch aptamers reach nanomolar affinity and discriminate close analogues. They are targets for antibiotics and support the RNA-world idea that RNA once combined genotype and phenotype roles.

title: Translation: initiation, elongation, termination
summary: The three stages of protein synthesis.

layers.basics: The ribosome assembles at a start codon, adds amino acids one by one as tRNAs match codons, and stops at a stop codon.
layers.deeper: Initiation uses Shine–Dalgarno (bacteria) or the 5′ cap and scanning (eukaryotes). Elongation cycles through A-site binding, peptide bond formation and translocation.
layers.expert: EF-Tu delivers tRNAs and GTP hydrolysis proofreads; error rate ≈ 10⁻⁴ per codon. Release factors recognise stop codons. Polysomes allow many ribosomes per mRNA.

title: Chromatin remodelling and the histone code
summary: Enzymes that read and rewrite chromatin.

layers.basics: Writer enzymes add marks to histones, eraser enzymes remove them and reader proteins recognise them, so chromatin can be opened or closed.
layers.deeper: ATP-driven remodelers slide or evict nucleosomes. Together they make genes accessible to transcription machinery.
layers.expert: The "histone code" hypothesis proposes combinatorial marks encode regulatory states; how instructive versus consequential marks are is debated. Polycomb and Trithorax complexes maintain repressed and active states.

open_questions: Which histone modifications cause, rather than follow, changes in transcription remains contested.

title: Genetic testing, counselling and screening
summary: Using genetics to inform health decisions.

layers.basics: Genetic tests check for carrier status, risk of disease, or conditions in embryos and newborns. Counsellors explain what the results mean.
layers.deeper: Newborn screening tests for dozens of treatable conditions (PKU, CF). Polygenic scores give modest risk predictions for common diseases.
layers.expert: Test performance (sensitivity, specificity, PPV) depends on prevalence; variants of uncertain significance (VUS) are common. Ethical issues include privacy, discrimination and embryo selection.

facts: Typical VUS rate in panel tests

layers.basics: Identical twins share all genes; fraternal twins share half. Comparing them estimates how much of a trait's variation is genetic.
layers.deeper: Falconer's formula h² ≈ 2(r_MZ − r_DZ). Twin studies suggest high heritability for height and moderate for many behaviours.
layers.expert: Assumptions (equal environments, no assortative mating) can fail; gene–environment correlation and interaction complicate interpretation. Molecular methods (GREML, GWAS) now complement twin designs.

layers.basics: Forward genetics starts from a mutant trait and finds the gene; reverse genetics starts from a gene and creates a mutant to see the effect.
layers.deeper: Screens in yeast, flies, worms and zebrafish found cell-cycle, development and signalling genes. CRISPR now lets researchers knock out every gene in a genome-wide screen.
layers.expert: Complementation tests group mutations into genes. Genome-wide CRISPR screens use pooled guides with sequencing readout and statistical tools (MAGeCK) to find essential genes (≈ 2,000 in human cell lines).

title: Roots, nutrient uptake and rhizosphere
summary: The underground half of the plant.

layers.basics: Roots anchor plants and take up water and nutrients through root hairs. The soil around roots (rhizosphere) is full of microbes.
layers.deeper: Mycorrhizal fungi extend the root's reach; nodules host nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legumes. Roots secrete acids and sugars to shape the rhizosphere.
layers.expert: The Casparian strip forces water and solutes through selective membranes in the endodermis. Total root length in a single rye plant has been estimated at > 600 km.

layers.basics: Plants make compounds not needed for basic growth but useful for defence and signalling: caffeine, nicotine, morphine, capsaicin and pigments.
layers.deeper: Many human medicines come from plants (aspirin, taxol, artemisinin, digitoxin).
layers.expert: Three main classes: terpenoids, phenolics and alkaloids. Metabolic gene clusters and coevolutionary arms races with herbivores shape diversity; ≈ 200,000 plant natural products are known.

layers.basics: Under drought, roots signal leaves, hormone abscisic acid builds up and stomata close to save water.
layers.deeper: Plants also respond to cold with antifreeze proteins and to salt by sequestering ions in vacuoles.
layers.expert: Osmolytes (proline, sucrose) lower water potential; heat shock proteins protect proteins. Breeding and engineering of stress tolerance is a major agricultural goal under climate change.

title: Crop domestication and plant breeding

layers.basics: Farmers selected wild plants over ≈ 10,000 years to make crops like wheat, rice and maize with larger seeds and less shattering.
layers.deeper: Modern breeding uses crosses, mutation breeding, marker-assisted selection and genome editing. Green Revolution dwarf wheat boosted yields.
layers.expert: Domestication syndrome genes (e.g., teosinte branched1 in maize, Rht in wheat) were identified by QTL mapping. Crop diversity narrows risk (Irish potato famine, banana TR4).

facts: Rice, wheat, maize share of calories

title: Plant pathogens and immunity
summary: Diseases of plants and how they fight back.

layers.basics: Fungi, bacteria, viruses and nematodes attack plants. Plants respond with physical barriers, chemicals and localised cell death.
layers.deeper: The hypersensitive response sacrifices infected cells. Resistance (R) genes recognise pathogen effectors.
layers.expert: Plants lack mobile immune cells but have PAMP-triggered and effector-triggered immunity. Wheat rust and rice blast threaten food security; durable resistance requires pyramiding R genes.

facts: Crop losses to pests and disease

layers.basics: Many plants have extra sets of chromosomes. Bread wheat has six sets and strawberries have eight.
layers.deeper: Polyploidy can instantly create new species and often gives larger organs; breeders use colchicine to double chromosomes.
layers.expert: Allopolyploids combine genomes of two species (e.g., Brassica napus). Roughly 30% of living plant species are recent polyploids and all flowering plants show ancient duplications.

layers.basics: Arachnids (spiders, scorpions, mites, ticks) have eight legs and two body regions. Crustaceans (crabs, shrimp, barnacles) mostly live in water and have two pairs of antennae.
layers.deeper: Ticks and mites spread diseases; krill form a keystone food source in the Southern Ocean.
layers.expert: Spider silk is a protein with tensile strength ≈ 1 GPa. Antarctic krill biomass is estimated at 100–500 million tonnes. Pancrustacean phylogeny places insects within crustaceans.

title: Parasites and helminths
summary: Life on and in other animals.

layers.basics: Parasites such as tapeworms, flukes and roundworms live in hosts and take nutrients. Some have complex life cycles with multiple hosts.
layers.deeper: About 1.5 billion people are infected with soil-transmitted worms. Schistosomiasis affects ≈ 240 million.
layers.expert: Parasites make up a large share of biodiversity, perhaps 40% of animal species. They manipulate host behaviour and immune responses; the hygiene hypothesis links reduced helminth exposure to allergy risk (still debated).

title: Evolution of flight and key innovations

layers.basics: Flight evolved independently in insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats. Each used different wing structures.
layers.deeper: Feathered dinosaurs show feathers came before flight; Archaeopteryx (≈ 150 Ma) shows a mix of reptile and bird features.
layers.expert: Hypotheses for bird flight origin include ground-up (running) and trees-down (gliding); evidence from wing-assisted incline running supports a mix. Flight requires high power-to-weight and efficient lungs.

open_questions: Whether bird flight arose from ground-up or arboreal origins is not settled.

layers.basics: Lichens are partnerships between fungi and algae or cyanobacteria that colonise bare rock. Yeasts and moulds are used to make bread, beer, antibiotics and enzymes.
layers.deeper: Lichens are sensitive to air pollution. Penicillium makes penicillin; Aspergillus makes citric acid industrially.
layers.expert: Saccharomyces cerevisiae is the first eukaryote with a fully sequenced genome (1996, ≈ 12 Mb, ≈ 6,000 genes). Fungal enzymes and mycoprotein are growing industries.

title: Protostome and deuterostome development
summary: Two ways to form a mouth.

layers.basics: In protostomes the first opening in the embryo (blastopore) becomes the mouth; in deuterostomes it becomes the anus.
layers.deeper: Humans and sea urchins are deuterostomes; insects and snails are protostomes. Cleavage patterns and coelom formation also differ.
layers.expert: Molecular phylogeny supports the split but shows exceptions to the textbook developmental differences. Xenacoelomorphs' position (basal or with deuterostomes) is still debated.

open_questions: The phylogenetic position of Xenacoelomorpha affects interpretations of early bilaterian evolution.

title: Countercurrent exchange and multiplication
summary: A recurring design for efficient transfer.

layers.basics: When two fluids flow in opposite directions side by side, heat or solutes can transfer along the whole length. Fish gills, bird legs and kidneys use this.
layers.deeper: Countercurrent heat exchange stops a duck's feet from losing body heat. In the kidney, the loop of Henle multiplies a salt gradient.
layers.expert: Countercurrent exchange can in principle transfer nearly 100% versus 50% for concurrent flow. Multiplication uses active transport to create a gradient larger than the single-step difference.

title: Acid–base and fluid balance in the body

layers.basics: The body holds blood pH steady using buffers, breathing (removes CO₂) and the kidneys (excrete acid or base).
layers.deeper: Respiratory acidosis follows CO₂ retention; metabolic acidosis may follow diabetic ketosis. Hormones ADH, aldosterone and ANP control water and sodium.
layers.expert: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for bicarbonate links pH to PCO₂ and [HCO₃⁻]. Compensation takes minutes (respiratory) to days (renal). Body water ≈ 60% of mass: two-thirds intracellular, one-third extracellular.

title: Blood pressure and cardiovascular regulation
summary: Keeping blood flowing at the right pressure.

layers.basics: Blood pressure depends on heart output and resistance in vessels. Nerves and hormones adjust both.
layers.deeper: Baroreceptors sense stretch and change heart rate; the kidneys regulate volume through the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.
layers.expert: MAP ≈ CO × SVR; CO = HR × SV. Normal adult values: ≈ 120/80 mmHg, CO ≈ 5 L/min. Hypertension affects ≈ 30% of adults and is controlled with drugs targeting RAAS, calcium channels or diuresis.

formula: MAP = CO × SVR;  CO = HR × SV

layers.basics: Muscles use stored ATP and creatine phosphate for seconds, glycolysis for minutes and aerobic metabolism for long efforts.
layers.deeper: Fast-twitch fibres suit sprinting and slow-twitch fibres suit endurance. Training raises mitochondria number and capillary density.
layers.expert: VO₂max (≈ 35–45 mL/kg/min untrained, > 80 in elite endurance athletes) is limited by cardiac output. Lactate threshold, oxygen debt and muscle fibre types predict performance.

title: Torpor, hibernation and extreme physiology
summary: Surviving cold, drought and low oxygen.

layers.basics: Some animals lower their metabolism and body temperature to save energy: bears, ground squirrels and hummingbirds.
layers.deeper: Arctic ground squirrels can cool to below 0 °C; wood frogs freeze solid and thaw. Tardigrades survive near-total dehydration.
layers.expert: Hibernators suppress metabolism to ≈ 2–5% of normal and preserve muscle by unknown mechanisms. Antifreeze proteins and cryoprotectants (glucose, glycerol) protect cells.

facts: Arctic ground squirrel min. body temp.

title: Cytokines and chemokines
summary: The messengers of the immune system.

layers.basics: Cytokines are small proteins that immune cells use to talk, such as interleukins and interferons. Chemokines guide cells to sites of infection.
layers.deeper: Too much cytokine release causes a "cytokine storm" in severe infections. Drugs that block TNF or IL-6 treat autoimmune disease.
layers.expert: Cytokines signal through JAK–STAT pathways; receptors share common chains. Interferons induce hundreds of antiviral genes. Pleiotropy and redundancy complicate therapeutic targeting.

title: Hematopoiesis: making blood cells

layers.basics: Blood cells are made in bone marrow from haematopoietic stem cells. These make red cells, platelets and all white cells.
layers.deeper: Erythropoietin from the kidney boosts red blood cell production; G-CSF boosts neutrophils. Bone marrow transplants replace diseased stem cells.
layers.expert: The tree splits into myeloid and lymphoid lineages; cell fate is controlled by transcription factors (GATA1, PU.1) and cytokines. About 2×10¹¹ red cells are made daily.

facts: Red blood cells made per day

layers.basics: Complement proteins in blood coat microbes so phagocytes eat them, and can punch holes in bacterial membranes.
layers.deeper: Three pathways (classical, lectin, alternative) converge on C3 cleavage. Inflammation signals C3a and C5a attract immune cells.
layers.expert: The membrane attack complex (C5b–C9) forms ≈ 10 nm pores. Complement deficiencies increase infections; excessive activation contributes to autoimmune and eye diseases (complement inhibitors approved).

title: Embryonic induction and the organiser
summary: Signals from one tissue direct another.

layers.basics: In 1924, Spemann and Mangold transplanted a small region of a newt embryo and showed it could organise a second body axis.
layers.deeper: Induction is when one group of cells signals to another to change its fate, as the lens is induced by the optic cup.
layers.expert: The organiser secretes BMP antagonists (noggin, chordin) that set up dorsal–ventral patterning. Spemann received the 1935 Nobel Prize. Induction principles are reused in organ formation.

title: Sex determination and gonad development
summary: How embryos become male or female.

layers.basics: In humans, the SRY gene on the Y chromosome switches the gonad towards testis; without it ovaries develop. Hormones then shape other tissues.
layers.deeper: Testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone direct male structures. Variations in sex development (DSD) arise from differences in genes, hormones or receptors.
layers.expert: SRY activates SOX9; WNT4/RSPO1/FOXL2 maintain ovarian identity. Other animals use temperature (many reptiles), chromosome counts (bees) or social cues (clownfish).

title: Axis formation and symmetry breaking
summary: Establishing front, back and left, right.

layers.basics: Early embryos need to know up from down and left from right. Maternal molecules and early signals break the initial symmetry.
layers.deeper: In flies, Bicoid and Nanos mRNAs are placed at opposite ends of the egg. In vertebrates, cilia generate flow that sets left–right asymmetry.
layers.expert: Nodal signalling and cilia-driven flow in the node break left–right symmetry; defects cause situs inversus. Symmetry breaking uses reaction–diffusion and mechanical feedback.

layers.basics: Cells stream one by one past lasers, and detectors record scattered and fluorescent light. This counts cell types and can sort them.
layers.deeper: Fluorescent antibodies label markers such as CD4 or CD8. Clinical uses include blood cell counts, leukaemia diagnosis and CD4 counts in HIV.
layers.expert: Instruments measure ≈ 10⁴ cells per second across ≥ 10–40 parameters; compensation corrects for spectral overlap. Gating strategies and controls (FMO) drive correct interpretation.

title: Calibration, standard curves and detection limits

layers.basics: To turn a signal into a concentration, you measure known standards, draw a calibration curve, and read unknowns from it.
layers.deeper: Include a blank and replicates. Keep unknowns within the linear range, or dilute them.
layers.expert: Limit of detection ≈ 3.3σ/slope and limit of quantitation ≈ 10σ/slope. Weighted regression handles heteroscedastic errors; four-parameter logistic fits are standard for ELISA.

title: Western blots and ELISA in practice
summary: From lysate to a quantified band or well.

layers.basics: In a Western blot, proteins are separated on a gel, moved onto a membrane and detected with antibodies. In an ELISA, antibodies capture and detect the target in a plate well.
layers.deeper: Loading controls (actin, tubulin) check equal loading. Validation of antibodies with knockout controls prevents false conclusions.
layers.expert: Quantitation requires signals in the linear range; saturated bands cannot be compared. Many published antibodies fail specificity tests, a recognised reproducibility problem.

title: Ecosystem stability, resilience and tipping points

layers.basics: Ecosystems can resist change, bounce back (resilience), or shift to a new state if pushed too far.
layers.deeper: Diverse communities often show more stable production over time (insurance effect). Lakes can flip from clear to algal-dominated.
layers.expert: Alternative stable states and hysteresis arise from feedbacks (Scheffer). Early-warning signals (critical slowing down) are proposed but difficult to apply in practice; evidence for global tipping points is mixed.

open_questions: How general and predictable ecological tipping points are remains uncertain.

title: Plant–animal interaction networks
summary: Webs of pollinators, plants and seed dispersers.

layers.basics: Plants and animals form webs of mutual benefit: bees pollinate flowers, birds and mammals disperse seeds.
layers.deeper: Networks tend to be nested: specialists interact with subsets of what generalists use, which may buffer against loss.
layers.expert: Network metrics (nestedness, modularity) link structure to robustness. Declines in pollinators (habitat loss, pesticides, disease) threaten ≈ 75% of leading crops to some degree.

title: Soil ecology and the soil food web

layers.basics: A handful of soil holds billions of microbes plus fungi, worms and mites. They break down organic matter and make nutrients available.
layers.deeper: Earthworms mix soil; fungi bind particles; bacteria fix nitrogen. Soil carbon is the largest terrestrial carbon store.
layers.expert: Soil holds ≈ 1,500–2,400 Pg C, about 2–3× atmospheric carbon. Soil carbon persistence depends more on mineral association and microbial processing than on chemical recalcitrance (the microbial carbon pump view).
